answers.question: What is the mechanism for?
answers.answer: It keeps the service's single log file from filling the disk by closing it from time to time, putting it aside under a dated name and starting a new one.
quotes: The service writes its log into one file, and a file that only grows fills the disk.
So the service closes the file from time to time, puts it aside under a dated name and starts a new one.

answers.question: What does it take in, and what does it keep?
answers.answer: It takes in one event, a line to be written, and keeps the size of the current file and the time it was opened.
quotes: The mechanism keeps the size of the current file and the time it was opened.
It takes in one event, a line to be written.

answers.question: By which steps does it reach its result?
answers.answer: Before each line it checks the current file against 100 megabytes and one day; under both it writes the line to the current file, over either it closes the file, renames it with the closing date and time, opens a new file and writes the line there.
quotes: Before each line the service checks the current file against two limits, 100 megabytes and one day.
Under both limits it writes the line into the current file.
Over either limit it closes the file and renames it with the date and time of closing.
It then opens a new file and writes the line there.
answers.missing: The text announces five steps and says it will explain what happens to the files put aside, but gives four steps and no step that limits the files put aside to seven, which the 800-megabyte result depends on.

answers.question: What does a reader see when it works, on the example the text gives?
answers.answer: The text says the put-aside files are named log.<date-time> and that the logs never take more than about 800 megabytes, seven files put aside and the current one.
quotes: So the logs never take more than about 800 megabytes: seven files put aside and the current one.
if over:      close the file; rename it to log.<date-time>
answers.missing: A worked example run through the steps: a file of a given size and age, the line that arrives, and the files a reader would then see on disk.

unexplained.quote: So the logs never take more than about 800 megabytes: seven files put aside and the current one.

retelling.step: When a line arrives, the service checks the current file against two limits: over if its size exceeds 100 megabytes or its age exceeds one day.
quotes: Before each line the service checks the current file against two limits, 100 megabytes and one day.
on a line:    over = size > 100 MB or age > 1 day

retelling.step: If the file is under both limits, the line is written into the current file.
quotes: Under both limits it writes the line into the current file.
if not over:  write the line to the current file

retelling.step: If the file is over either limit, the service closes it and renames it with the date and time of closing, as log.<date-time>.
quotes: Over either limit it closes the file and renames it with the date and time of closing.
if over:      close the file; rename it to log.<date-time>

retelling.step: It then opens a new file and writes the line into it.
quotes: It then opens a new file and writes the line there.
open a new file; write the line to it

gaps: No step does anything with the renamed files after they are put aside, yet the result says only seven are kept: the text would have to say which step removes or limits the older put-aside files.
The text says the mechanism is five steps and that it explains what happens to the files put aside, but the steps given are four and none of them handles the files put aside.
